families.source: UKHSA guidance for people exposed to birds or animals infected with influenza A(H5)
families.topic: prevention, exposure assessment, PPE, follow-up, symptomatic management and public-health case definitions for influenza A(H5)
families.page_title: Guidance for the management of people exposed to birds or other animals infected with influenza A(H5)
evidence_points: The guidance covers public-health management of people exposed to birds or other animals infected with influenza A(H5).
It sets out principles for preventing human infection following animal incidents.
It distinguishes animal case definitions from human exposure assessment.
It describes personal protective equipment considerations for work involving suspected or infected animals.
It provides management pathways for people assessed as exposed.
It provides a separate pathway for symptomatic people with relevant animal exposure.
It includes public-health case definitions for health protection teams.
It links exposure management with diagnostic testing and interpretation of results.
Animal contact alone does not establish human infection with influenza A(H5).
Final action requires exposure intensity, PPE, symptoms, timing, laboratory evidence and current health-protection assessment.

families.source: UKHSA diagnostic testing guidance for avian influenza A(H5) and other zoonotic influenza viruses
families.topic: clinical sampling, laboratory referral, subtype testing, confirmatory testing, reporting and interpretation for suspected zoonotic influenza
families.page_title: Diagnostic testing for avian influenza A(H5) and other zoonotic influenza viruses
evidence_points: The guidance covers taking, submitting and processing samples from suspected zoonotic influenza cases.
It is intended for clinicians, healthcare workers, health protection teams and diagnostic laboratories.
Testing strategy depends on symptoms and relevant exposure to birds or mammals in the UK or overseas.
Clinical Network Laboratories perform influenza A typing and subtyping tests including H5.
Confirmatory testing and characterisation are performed by the National Influenza Reference Laboratory.
Testing includes seasonal H1 and H3 alongside H5 where specified.
Sample transport, referral and result communication follow defined laboratory pathways.
Confirmatory positive results have explicit notification and reporting requirements.
A negative local influenza A result alone may not exclude zoonotic influenza when exposure criteria remain strong.
Interpretation requires specimen quality, timing, exposure history, assay scope and confirmatory laboratory evidence.

families.source: UKHSA Lyme disease management and prevention guidance
families.topic: clinical management, transmission, tick-bite prevention and limits of post-exposure prophylaxis for Lyme disease
evidence_points: Prompt recognition and a full course of appropriate antibiotics usually resolves acute Lyme disease.
An erythema migrans rash can be treated on clinical suspicion without waiting for laboratory confirmation.
Other possible manifestations should be recognised and investigated according to the clinical presentation.
The guidance points healthcare professionals to NICE recommendations for treatment.
Post-exposure prophylaxis is not recommended in the UK.
Prevention focuses on tick awareness, reducing tick bites and prompt correct tick removal.
There is no reliable documented evidence of person-to-person Lyme disease transmission.
No human Lyme disease vaccine is currently available for routine prevention.
A tick bite, even from an infected tick, does not necessarily result in Lyme disease.
Management requires symptoms, examination, exposure geography, timing and appropriate laboratory or specialist assessment.

families.source: UKHSA Rare and Imported Pathogens Laboratory Lyme disease services
families.topic: local and reference laboratory testing, confirmatory serology, neurological Lyme testing and specialist advice
evidence_points: First-line Lyme testing may be available through local NHS laboratory services.
UKHSA's Rare and Imported Pathogens Laboratory provides confirmatory diagnostic testing.
Lyme disease is usually investigated using serology.
The reference service uses a modified two-tier testing approach.
The initial screen combines IgG and IgM antibody detection.
The service provides diagnostic and advisory support to healthcare professionals.
Specialist testing is available for suspected neurological Lyme disease.
Clinical details and appropriate specimens are needed for meaningful laboratory interpretation.
An antibody result alone does not establish that current symptoms are caused by active Lyme disease.
Interpretation requires clinical presentation, exposure history, timing, prior treatment and the complete testing algorithm.

families.source: UKHSA Lyme disease sample testing advice
families.topic: access to NHS testing, specialist discussion, accredited confirmatory testing and sample interpretation
evidence_points: The testing advice is intended for healthcare professionals in the UK.
Patients concerned about possible infection are directed to an appropriate healthcare professional.
Healthcare professionals should use local infection-specialist advice and local testing arrangements.
NHS Lyme testing is available through local providers and the UKHSA reference laboratory.
The reference laboratory provides accredited confirmatory testing.
The service also supports investigation of neurological Lyme disease.
Testing decisions should reflect the patient's symptoms and likely exposure.
Sample timing and the stage of illness affect the value of antibody testing.
A single negative or positive result should not be interpreted without the clinical context and test stage.
Final interpretation requires the complete algorithm, specimen timing, symptoms, exposure and specialist advice where needed.
